storySeeds.title: The Southern Cross: a family, an impostor and our nearest neighbour
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: Are the stars of a constellation really neighbours?
storySeeds.notes: Mimosa (probable LCC, ~16 Myr) → Jewel Box 1° away (same age, 23× farther) → δ Cru (secure LCC member) → Acrux (debated member) → Gacrux twist (foreground red giant, 89 ly vs ~280–460 ly) → Hadar → Alpha Centauri payoff (4.4 ly, LINE_OF_SIGHT with Hadar). Everything within ~12° of Crux; Coalsack can be a coda. Mirrors the Southern Cross / Pointers / Jewel Box core of the Astronomical League Southern Skies binocular list.

storySeeds.title: Carina and Vela: how heavy stars live and die
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: What happens to the heaviest stars?
storySeeds.notes: θ Car and the Southern Pleiades (a ~46 Myr family) → η Car (twist: the fainter star is 16× farther and far more powerful; LBV, Great Eruption) → Carina Nebula it lights → ζ Pup (O supergiant, runaway, 40,000 K) → γ² Vel (Wolf–Rayet stripped core; binocular double) → Suhail (cool red supergiant, alternative ending). Region spans ~35°; split into a Carina half and a Puppis–Vela half if the cap is tight.

storySeeds.title: The Sun’s life story, told by its southern cousins
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: What will happen to the Sun?
storySeeds.notes: β Pic (a 23 Myr star still making planets: the Sun’s infancy) → α Cen A (a near-solar twin, 4.5–5.3 Gyr: the Sun today) → β Hyi (6.5 Gyr subgiant: the Sun in ~2 Gyr) → L² Pup (AGB, 0.66 M☉, ESO’s ‘glimpse of the Sun’s future’) → NGC 2438 (planetary nebula, challenge). Too spread for one region; best as two regional variants: Pictor–Puppis (β Pic, L² Pup, NGC 2438) and Centaurus–Hydrus (α Cen, β Hyi).

storySeeds.title: Strangers near Canopus: a runaway, a halo visitor and a planet nursery
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: Do all stars belong where we see them?
storySeeds.notes: Canopus (bright because powerful, 310 ly) → β Pic 6° away (5× closer, fainter; 23 Myr with imaged planets) → Kapteyn’s Star (challenge; ancient halo red dwarf, 8.6″/yr) → NGC 1851 5° away (a whole ball of halo stars) → Phact → μ Col 2° away (runaway ejected from the Orion Nebula Cluster 2.5 Myr ago). All within ~20° of Columba/Pictor.

card.question: What is the nearest star system you can see with the naked eye?
card.glance: The outer of the two bright Pointers beside the Southern Cross, in Centaurus, a single dazzling yellow-white point.
card.whyHere: Alpha Centauri is the closest star system your eyes can reach, and the yardstick for every other distance in the southern sky.
card.see: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show one brilliant point, because its two Sun-like stars sit too close to separate without a telescope. Compare its warm tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
card.understand: Its distance was among the first ever measured, by parallax: as Earth swings around the Sun, a near star shifts slightly against the far ones, and the smaller the shift, the farther the star. Alpha Centauri’s shift is the largest of any naked-eye star, under a second of arc, about the width of a coin seen from several kilometers. Behind that one point are two stars circling every 80 years, one nearly a twin of our Sun and one a smaller orange star.
card.wonder: If the Sun were a 1 cm marble, Earth would be a grain of sand a meter away, and Alpha Centauri another marble about 300 km away.
card.connect: Hadar, the other Pointer, looks almost as bright yet belongs to a completely different league of stars.
card.answer: Alpha Centauri, whose light takes about 4.4 years to reach you. Its faint third member, the red dwarf Proxima, is closer still, the nearest single star of all.
card.photoCaption: Photos show one overexposed glare; only a telescope splits the two stars, and Proxima lies well outside the frame.
card.notSee: You will not see the two stars separately, nor Proxima or its planet.
card.deeper: VLTI/PIONIER interferometry measured the stars’ disks (8.50 and 6.00 mas); with a parallax of 747.17 ± 0.61 mas this gives radii of 1.223 and 0.863 R☉ (Kervella et al. 2017). Ten years of HARPS velocities plus the visual orbit yield masses of about 1.13 and 0.97 M☉ and a 79.91-year period (Pourbaix & Boffin 2016). Spectroscopy puts A near 5,820 K and the pair at 4.5–5.3 billion years, close to the Sun’s age (Porto de Mello et al. 2008). The pair moves 3.7″ per year across the sky.

card.question: Is the Pointer that looks like Alpha Centauri’s twin really nearby too?
card.glance: The Pointer nearer the Southern Cross, in Centaurus, a brilliant blue-white point.
card.whyHere: Hadar stands beside Alpha Centauri as if the two were a matched pair, and the truth behind that pairing is a lesson in power.
card.see: Swing between the two Pointers: Hadar is blue-white, Alpha Centauri warmer and yellower. In binoculars Hadar stays a single point, because its three stars sit far too close together to split.
card.understand: Hadar is a hot, young triple, and its two main stars, about 12 and 11 times the Sun’s mass, circle each other almost exactly once a year. Watching that orbit both on the sky and in the shifting colors of their light gives its true size in kilometers and its size in angle, and comparing the two yields a distance. That orbital parallax puts Hadar about 361 light-years away, far more precisely than the Hipparcos satellite managed.
card.wonder: The light now reaching you from Hadar left around 1665, when Isaac Newton was a student.
card.connect: Stars this heavy do not live long, and their young relatives crowd the Southern Cross next door.
card.answer: Hadar lies far beyond its partner Pointer and rivals Alpha Centauri only because its heavy, hot stars pour out enormous power, so the Pointers are a pair only from where we stand.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only glare; the pair inside Hadar was separated by linking telescopes together (interferometry).
card.notSee: Its companions are invisible in binoculars.
card.deeper: Pigulski et al. (2016) combined BRITE nanosatellite photometry with interferometric and spectroscopic orbits: masses 12.02 ± 0.13 and 10.58 ± 0.18 M☉, period 356.9 d, and an orbital parallax of 9.04 ± 0.04 mas (110.6 ± 0.5 pc), against 8.32 ± 0.50 mas from Hipparcos. Both components fit a 10–15 Myr isochrone and pulsate in β Cephei and slowly-pulsating-B modes. Its membership in the Lower Centaurus–Crux group of Sco-Cen is debated (Preibisch & Mamajek 2008).

card.question: How can a star 310 light-years away outshine almost every other star?
card.glance: The second-brightest star of the night, in Carina, a dazzling white point well south of Sirius.
card.whyHere: Canopus outshines nearly everything in the night sky from about 310 light-years, so its brilliance must come from power rather than closeness.
card.see: Canopus needs no finder: it is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers through colors as our air splits its light, while higher up it is a steady white. Sweep about 6° west to faint Beta Pictoris, a star five times closer, for perspective.
card.understand: Interferometers combine telescopes to measure the tiny disk of Canopus, about 7 thousandths of an arcsecond across. Knowing the distance, that angle becomes a true width of roughly 73 Suns. A surface that large and that hot must shine fiercely, and its total light, measured across all colors, confirms it: about 16,000 times the Sun’s output.
card.wonder: Spacecraft have long steered by Canopus, because it is bright and sits far from the Sun’s path across the sky.
card.connect: Bright does not mean near: faint Beta Pictoris, 6° away, is five times closer.
card.answer: Canopus simply pours out power, a giant of nine or ten Suns’ mass swollen past its long, steady adult life and probably now burning helium in its core, and few stars in our part of the galaxy match it.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only glare; Canopus’s true disk has been measured only by linking telescopes together.
card.deeper: Domiciano de Souza et al. (2021) measured a limb-darkened diameter of 7.184 mas with VLTI/PIONIER and combined it with the Hipparcos distance (94.8 ± 5.0 pc): R = 73 ± 4 R☉, Teff ≈ 7,660 K, log L/L☉ = 4.22. Geneva tracks give 9–10 M☉ and 24–34 Myr, placing Canopus most likely on the core-helium-burning ‘blue loop’. The ~5% distance error dominates the radius uncertainty.

card.question: What happens to a star that spins almost fast enough to fly apart?
card.glance: An icy blue-white star shining alone, low in the far south.
card.whyHere: Achernar is one of the fastest-spinning bright stars in the sky, turning so quickly that it is squashed into a flattened ball.
card.see: Look for the lone brilliant blue-white star at the end of the long, faint river of Eridanus. Binoculars show only a sharp point, so enjoy its icy color and compare it with creamy Alpha Hydri about 5° away.
card.understand: Achernar is a hot star about six times the Sun’s mass, spinning near the speed at which it would fling itself apart. As with a spinning pizza dough, the spin pushes its equator outward into a bulge. Interferometers at the VLT combined telescopes to measure its outline and found it longer one way than the other, the flattest star resolved at the time.
card.wonder: It is only about 63 million years old, while the Sun has already lived some 70 times longer.
card.connect: A smaller companion swings around it every seven years, and its orbit is how astronomers weighed Achernar.
card.answer: It flattens and leaks, Achernar’s equator bulging about a third wider than its poles and, from time to time, shedding a thin disk of gas from that waist. Pushed far enough, a star starts to come apart at the seams.
card.photoCaption: No photo shows its shape; the flattening was measured by linking telescopes together (interferometry).
card.notSee: Its flattened shape and its companion are far beyond binoculars.
card.deeper: VLTI interferometry resolved Achernar’s flattened shape; Domiciano de Souza et al. (2014) found an equatorial-to-polar radius ratio near 1.35, the flattest such star then resolved. Kervella et al. (2022) followed the A-type companion through a 7-year, highly eccentric orbit (e = 0.73): 6.0 ± 0.6 M☉ for the Be star, and a critically rotating 6.4 M☉ model at 63 Myr fits best. At 42.8 pc it is the nearest Be star; a comoving low-mass star suggests membership of the Tucana–Horologium moving group.

card.question: What does a star on the brink of exploding look like?
card.glance: A small yellow-orange star buried in the bright Carina Nebula, whose brightness changes over the years.
card.whyHere: Eta Carinae is one of the most massive and unstable stars known, and almost certain to end as a supernova one day.
card.see: Center the Carina Nebula, the brightest patch of the southern Milky Way. Near its brightest part sits a compact star with a warmer, yellow-orange tint than its white neighbors, and that is Eta Carinae. It looks ordinary; the drama lies in what it is.
card.understand: Eta Carinae is a pair of giant stars circling every five and a half years, and the heavier may once have weighed as much as 150 Suns. In the 1840s it blew off more than ten Suns’ worth of gas and survived, and that gas now forms a twin-lobed cloud, the Homunculus. Measuring how fast the cloud expands and how large it looks gives its distance, like judging a balloon by its growth.
card.wonder: For a few years it was the second-brightest star in the night sky, even though its light travels about 7,500 years to reach us.
card.connect: Stars this heavy shed their outer layers before they die, and Gamma Velorum, in neighboring Vela, holds a star that already has.
card.answer: It looks surprisingly ordinary, a small yellow-orange point dimmed and reddened by the very cloud it blew off in the 1840s, and that quiet look hides a star that once nearly tore itself apart.
card.photoCaption: Hubble’s photos show the Homunculus, two billowing lobes of gas and dust that no binocular can show.
card.notSee: The Homunculus is far too small to see in binoculars.
card.deeper: The expansion of the Homunculus gives a distance of 2.35 ± 0.05 kpc (Smith 2006). A 2,022.7 ± 1.3-day cycle in spectra and X-rays reveals a massive companion on an eccentric orbit (Damineli et al. 2008). Hubble ultraviolet imaging traces gas launched in the Great Eruption, estimated at more than ten solar masses (ESA/Hubble heic1912). Because dust in the Homunculus dims and reddens the star, its apparent brightness says little about its true output; it has brightened markedly since the 1990s.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness has changed by many times since the 1840s and is still changing; check AAVSO for its current brightness instead of relying on a fixed value.

card.question: What is left when a heavy star’s winds strip it to the core?
card.glance: Vela’s brightest star, with a fainter companion 41 arcseconds away that steady 10× binoculars split.
card.whyHere: Gamma Velorum holds a rare Wolf–Rayet star, the stripped-bare core of a heavy star near the end of its life.
card.see: Steady your binoculars and Gamma Velorum splits into a bright white star with a fainter one just beside it. A little farther out, two much fainter stars complete a tiny group.
card.understand: The bright star is itself two stars in a 78-day orbit: a hot giant about 28 times the Sun’s mass and a Wolf–Rayet star of about 9. A Wolf–Rayet star is a heavy star whose fierce winds have blown away its outer hydrogen, exposing hot inner layers rich in carbon. Astronomers weighed both by following the orbit with an interferometer and with the shifting lines of their spectra.
card.wonder: Around it lie hundreds of faint newborn stars, a family only 5–10 million years old, all about 1,100 light-years away.
card.connect: Naos, next door in Puppis, is a heavyweight still wrapped in its hydrogen, the earlier stage of the same life.
card.answer: A Wolf–Rayet star is what remains, and Gamma Velorum’s smaller star, stripped to its hot inner layers, was once far heavier. It will probably end as a supernova.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the bright pair and a scatter of fainter stars; the Wolf–Rayet’s winds are revealed only by spectra.
card.notSee: The two stars inside γ² Vel cannot be separated in any binocular.
card.deeper: North et al. (2007) resolved the WR + O binary with the SUSI interferometer and combined it with spectroscopy: distance 336 (+8/−7) pc, M(O) = 28.5 ± 1.1 M☉, R(O) = 17 ± 2 R☉ and M(WR) = 9.0 ± 0.6 M☉. Jeffries et al. (2009) found a few hundred low-mass pre-main-sequence stars clustered around γ Vel, 5–10 Myr old by low-mass models but 3–4 Myr by high-mass models, a tension still discussed. γ² Vel is a member of Vela OB2 (de Zeeuw et al. 1999).

card.question: How hot can a star you see with your eyes be?
card.glance: A steely blue-white star in a rich Milky Way field in Puppis.
card.whyHere: Naos sits at the hot end of the stellar thermometer, with a surface about seven times hotter than the Sun’s.
card.see: In binoculars Naos is a sharp, steely blue-white point among many fainter Milky Way stars. Swing about 10° west to Pi Puppis, a deep yellow-orange star, and you have both ends of the temperature scale in neighboring fields.
card.understand: A star’s temperature is written in its spectrum: certain atoms only show their lines when hot enough to lose electrons, and Naos shows lines of helium stripped of an electron, a sign of extreme heat. Naos is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with about 25 times the Sun’s mass. It pours out roughly 450,000 times the Sun’s light, most of it ultraviolet.
card.wonder: It also races through space, probably thrown out of its birth cluster.
card.connect: Gamma Velorum, next door in Vela, shows what such a star becomes once its outer layers are stripped away.
card.answer: About 40,000 K, nearly seven times the Sun’s surface temperature, and most of its enormous output is ultraviolet light your eyes cannot see. What reaches you is only the visible tail of a far greater glare.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a bright blue-white point; its ultraviolet glare is recorded only by space telescopes.
card.deeper: Howarth & van Leeuwen (2019) re-examined the Hipparcos parallax (3.01 ± 0.10 mas; 332 ± 11 pc) and derived Teff ≈ 40 kK, log L/L☉ = 5.65, R ≈ 13.5 R☉ and a spectroscopic mass of 25 ± 5 M☉, below single-star predictions. Its runaway velocity (~56 km/s), rapid rotation (v sin i ≈ 213 km/s) and anomalous parameters suggest past binary interaction; Trumpler 10 is a candidate birthplace.

card.question: Do the stars of the Southern Cross really belong together?
card.glance: The foot of the Southern Cross, a dazzling blue-white point with a fainter star beside it.
card.whyHere: Acrux is the brightest star of the Southern Cross and the place to ask whether the Cross is a family or a coincidence.
card.see: Acrux is the bright star at the bottom of the Cross, and binoculars show a much fainter star beside it. The two brilliant stars that make up Acrux itself sit too close for binoculars, though a small telescope splits them.
card.understand: Stars born together drift through space together, so astronomers test family ties by measuring each star’s motion across the sky and its distance. Delta Crucis, and probably Mimosa, share the motion of a scattered family of hot young stars called an association. Acrux seems to belong too, though its measured motion fits less neatly, and the debate continues.
card.wonder: The brighter of the two stars inside Acrux is itself a pair that only its spectrum reveals, so this one point of light holds at least three stars.
card.connect: Swing up to Gacrux at the top of the Cross and compare the colors: a blue-white family and an orange stranger.
card.answer: Mostly they do: Acrux probably shares a scattered family born about 16 million years ago with Mimosa and Delta Crucis, while orange Gacrux, at the top, is a nearer stranger that only lines up with them.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the glare of Acrux with its fainter neighbor; the close pair inside it needs a telescope.
card.deeper: WDS lists the A–B pair (DUN 252) at 3.5″ and a 4.8-magnitude star, C, at 89″. The combined Hipparcos parallax is 10.13 ± 0.50 mas (≈ 320 ly). In the Sco-Cen review by Preibisch & Mamajek (2008), α Cru is one of six bright stars whose membership of the Lower Centaurus–Crux group (mean age ~16 Myr, ~118 pc) has been debated because their Hipparcos proper motions do not match well.

radiusRsun.note: intensity-interferometer diameter 0.722 ± 0.022 mas (Hanbury Brown et al. 1974) × Hipparcos distance

ageMyr.note: mean age of the Lower Centaurus–Crux group it probably belongs to

card.question: Can a star and a cluster born at the same time sit side by side?
card.glance: The eastern arm of the Southern Cross, a blue-white star and your signpost to the Jewel Box.
card.whyHere: Mimosa is a hot young star with a star cluster of the same age sitting right beside it in the sky.
card.see: Mimosa is the bright blue-white star on the Cross’s eastern arm. Place it at the edge of your view and look about 1° south-east, where a tight, glittering knot of stars appears: the Jewel Box, whose brightest stars share Mimosa’s icy color.
card.understand: Mimosa is a heavy, hot star that swells and shrinks very slightly several times a day, too little for your eye to notice. Its motion through space suggests it belongs to a scattered family of stars born together about 16 million years ago. The Jewel Box is dated separately, from its own brightest stars, and lands at a similar age.
card.wonder: You hold two families of the same age in one binocular view, one spread across the sky around you and one packed into a distant jewel.
card.connect: Gacrux, the orange star at the top of the Cross, is the one star here that does not belong with the others.
card.answer: They can, for Mimosa and the Jewel Box are both about 16 million years old, yet the Jewel Box lies more than twenty times farther away: the same birthday at very different addresses.
card.photoCaption: Photos show Mimosa beside the Jewel Box cluster; the cluster’s colored stars need a telescope to stand out.
card.deeper: Mimosa is a β Cephei pulsator (main period about 0.24 d, amplitude under 0.1 mag, GCVS). Its angular diameter from the Narrabri intensity interferometer (0.722 ± 0.022 mas) and the Hipparcos distance give about 6.6 R☉. Preibisch & Mamajek (2008) note that long-baseline proper motions favor its membership of Lower Centaurus–Crux (mean age ~16 Myr). The Jewel Box (NGC 4755) has a similar age but lies about 6,500 ly away.

radiusRsun.note: JSDC photometric diameter 28.05 ± 1.65 mas × Hipparcos distance

multiplicity.systemNote: The 6th-magnitude star 2.2′ away is a background star (chance alignment).

superlatives.claim: by far the closest of the Southern Cross’s bright stars

card.question: Why is the top star of the Southern Cross orange when the others are blue-white?
card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross, the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.whyHere: Gacrux looks like part of the Cross’s family, but it is a stranger, a nearby red giant that only lines up with the others.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot; defocus slightly and the color jumps out. A faint white star just to the north-east is a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant, a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. Its parallax is several times larger than those of the other Cross stars, which places it much nearer to us.
card.wonder: Its light set out less than a century ago, while the blue-white stars behind it sent theirs centuries earlier.
card.connect: Giants like this one end by puffing away their outer layers into a glowing shell, a planetary nebula, around a hot dying core.
card.answer: Gacrux is not one of the Cross’s blue-white family at all: it is an old red giant three to five times closer than the others. The Cross is a family photo with a neighbor standing in front.
card.photoCaption: In photos Gacrux looks like a member of the Cross; only distance measurements reveal it is in the foreground.
card.deeper: Hipparcos (van Leeuwen 2007) gives 36.83 ± 0.18 mas (88.6 ly), against roughly 280–460 ly for Mimosa, δ Cru and Acrux. An SED fit (McDonald et al. 2017) gives about 3,700 K and 860 L☉; the JSDC photometric diameter (28 mas) implies about 82 R☉. Its exact evolutionary phase (first-ascent giant or early asymptotic giant) is not settled. The 6.4-mag star 2.2′ away is optical (WDS).

ageMyr.note: age of the β Pictoris moving group, 23 ± 3 Myr

exoplanets.method: direct imaging (b); radial velocity, then imaged (c)

superlatives.claim: the first star around which a dusty planet-forming disk was photographed (1984)

historyHook.text: In 1984 a telescope blocking the star’s glare revealed a thin, edge-on disk of dust: the first such disk ever photographed.

images.caption: VLT infrared images taken in 2003 and 2009 with the star’s light removed, showing the planet β Pictoris b on opposite sides of its star.

card.question: What does a planetary system look like while it is still forming?
card.glance: A modest white star in faint Pictor, about 6° west of brilliant Canopus.
card.whyHere: Beta Pictoris is a young star still building its planets, with two giant worlds and a dusty disk around it.
card.see: Start at Canopus and sweep about 6° west to a lone, modest white star in an empty-looking area. Nothing in binoculars hints at its planets, so the wonder lies in knowing what is there.
card.understand: Beta Pictoris is only about 23 million years old, a toddler among stars. In 1984 astronomers blocked its glare with a disk inside the telescope and saw, for the first time around any star, a thin, edge-on disk of dust and rock, a young version of the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune. Two giant planets, each several times Jupiter’s mass, have since been photographed inside it.
card.wonder: Comets seem to plunge toward Beta Pictoris constantly, their evaporating gas showing up as fleeting marks in its spectrum.
card.connect: Kapteyn’s Star, in the same constellation, is the opposite, one of the oldest stars nearby and a visitor from the halo.
card.answer: It looks like Beta Pictoris, a young star wrapped in a flat disk of dust and rock with giant planets already formed inside it, much as our own Solar System must have looked long ago.
card.photoCaption: Telescope images remove the star’s glare to reveal the planet; such pictures take the largest telescopes, not binoculars.
card.notSee: The disk and planets are invisible in any amateur instrument.
card.deeper: Smith & Terrile (1984) imaged the edge-on debris disk with a coronagraph, after IRAS found its infrared excess. Planet b was imaged with VLT/NACO (Lagrange et al. 2009, 2010; ESO eso1024). Planet c, first found by radial velocities, was confirmed with VLTI/GRAVITY: 8.2 ± 0.8 Jupiter masses at 2.7 au, temperature about 1,250 K (Nowak et al. 2020). The parent moving group is 23 ± 3 Myr old (Mamajek & Bell 2014).

distanceLy.note: parallax 1.7024 ± 0.0898 mas; spectroscopic distance 581 pc agrees (Aschenbrenner et al. 2023)

superlatives.claim: one of the two classic runaway stars flung out of the Orion Nebula’s cluster

historyHook.text: Trace its path backwards, and that of AE Aurigae, and both lead to the Orion Nebula’s cluster about 2.5 million years ago.

card.question: Can a star be thrown out of the cluster where it was born?
card.glance: A faint bluish star about 2° from Phact in Columba, easy in binoculars and hard to pick out by eye.
card.whyHere: Mu Columbae is a stellar escapee, thrown out of the Orion Nebula’s star cluster and still racing away.
card.see: Find Phact, the brightest star of Columba, the Dove, south of Orion, and nudge about 2° north-east to the faint bluish-white star there. Nothing about it looks special, because its story is in its motion.
card.understand: Astronomers measure a star’s speed across the sky and toward or away from us, and from those they can run its path backward like a film in reverse. Run back Mu Columbae and AE Aurigae, in the northern sky, and both lead to the young cluster at the heart of the Orion Nebula about 2.5 million years ago. Computer simulations show how: two pairs of stars came too close, and in the gravitational tangle two were flung out in opposite directions.
card.wonder: It is about 19 times the Sun’s mass and 44,000 times as bright, yet it looks faint because it is about 1,900 light-years away.
card.connect: The cluster that threw them out still shines in Orion’s sword.
card.answer: It can, and a close encounter in the Orion Nebula’s cluster flung Mu Columbae one way and AE Aurigae the other, each at more than 100 km/s, proof that stellar nurseries can be rough places.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an ordinary bluish star; its speed is revealed only by careful position and spectrum measurements.
card.deeper: Hybrid non-LTE spectroscopy gives Teff = 33,400 ± 300 K, 18.9 M☉, 6.3 R☉ and log L/L☉ = 4.64, with a spectroscopic distance of 581 pc matching Gaia (Aschenbrenner et al. 2023). N-body simulations by Gualandris et al. (2004) reproduce μ Col and AE Aur as products of a binary–binary encounter in the Trapezium about 2.5 Myr ago that also left ι Ori as an eccentric binary; both runaways move at over 100 km/s.

radiusRsun.note: VLTI diameter 0.692 ± 0.06 mas (Ségransan et al. 2003) × Gaia distance

periodDays.note: stellar rotation period from Gaussian-process fit

exoplanets.method: radial velocity (claimed planets later attributed to stellar rotation)

superlatives.claim: the nearest known star belonging to the Galaxy’s ancient halo

historyHook.text: Some stars in its moving group share the chemistry of Omega Centauri, hinting that they were stripped from that giant cluster long ago.

card.question: Can a star from the galaxy’s ancient halo pass right by the Sun?
card.glance: A faint reddish dot in Pictor near the threshold of 50 mm binoculars, which needs a detailed chart.
card.whyHere: Kapteyn’s Star is a visitor from the galaxy’s ancient halo, passing close to the Sun on a path unlike that of its neighbors.
card.see: This is a challenge: use the app’s chart at high zoom and star-hop from the faint stars of Pictor. Kapteyn’s Star is a dim, slightly reddish point, among the faintest in the field, and once found it is one of the oldest stars you will ever see.
card.understand: Most nearby stars, like the Sun, circle the galaxy in its flat disk, moving together like cars in one lane. Kapteyn’s Star moves at a steep angle to that traffic, darting across our sky faster than almost any other star and receding at about 245 km/s. That motion marks it as a member of the halo, a sparse cloud of ancient stars, and its spectrum agrees: it is poor in heavy elements, made before the galaxy had forged many.
card.wonder: It crosses about a Moon’s width of sky every 220 years, a dash across the background stars by astronomical standards.
card.connect: Another halo resident, a whole ball of ancient stars, sits a few degrees away: the globular cluster NGC 1851.
card.answer: Kapteyn’s Star is doing it now, a red dwarf only 13 light-years away on a steep, looping halo orbit, passing through our neighborhood at high speed. It will not stay long by galactic standards.
card.photoCaption: Photos taken decades apart show it shifting against background stars; a single photo shows a faint red dot.
card.notSee: Its motion is far too slow to see during one night.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 gives a parallax of 254.20 mas (12.8 ly) and a proper motion of 8.65″/yr, among the largest of any star. Its radial velocity is about +245 km/s (Guinan et al. 2016). Planets reported by Anglada-Escudé et al. (2014) were later attributed to stellar rotation (125-day period) by Bortle et al. (2021). Wylie-de Boer et al. (2010) found that most stars of the Kapteyn moving group chemically resemble ω Centauri, possibly tidal debris from it.

massMsun.note: from solar-like oscillations and interferometric radius

radiusRsun.note: VLTI diameter 1.89 ± 0.02 mas (Kervella et al. 2004) × distance

ageMyr.note: 3.5 (+0.8/−1.3) Gyr as quoted by Matthews et al.

exoplanets.method: radial velocity + astrometry; imaged by JWST in 2023–24

components.label: Ba/Bb
components.notes: pair of brown dwarfs about 400″ away

multiplicity.systemNote: Wide brown-dwarf binary ε Ind Ba/Bb (far too faint for any amateur instrument) shares the star’s motion.

superlatives.claim: one of the closest stars with a directly photographed planet

historyHook.text: In 2024 the James Webb Space Telescope photographed its cold giant planet, a world at about the temperature of a winter’s day on Earth.

images.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Elisabeth Matthews (MPIA)
images.license: NASA media guidelines (public domain); ESA/Webb CC BY 4.0
images.caption: Webb mid-infrared image with the star’s light blocked; the planet ε Indi Ab is the small glow beside the masked star.

card.question: Why does one of our nearest neighbors look fainter than a distant star?
card.glance: A modest orange star in faint Indus, easy in binoculars and dim to the naked eye.
card.whyHere: Epsilon Indi is one of the Sun’s closest neighbors and host to a giant planet that has been photographed directly.
card.see: Ten degrees from brilliant Alnair, the bright star of Grus, Epsilon Indi looks like an unremarkable faint star. In binoculars notice its soft orange tint, warmer than Alnair’s blue-white.
card.understand: Epsilon Indi is an orange dwarf, smaller, cooler and fainter than the Sun, only about 12 light-years away. How bright a star looks mixes two things, its true power and its distance, and here they pull in opposite directions. Its gentle oscillations, measured like the ringing of a bell, give its mass, a little over three-quarters of the Sun’s.
card.wonder: The Webb telescope has imaged a planet several times Jupiter’s mass orbiting it, with a temperature near 2 °C.
card.connect: Alpha Centauri is closer still, and bright enough to see from a city.
card.answer: Epsilon Indi is a small orange dwarf giving out little light, while Alnair looks brighter because it is far more powerful, even from about eight times farther, so here the faint one is the near one.
card.photoCaption: Webb’s infrared image blocks the star to reveal the cold planet; binoculars show only the orange star.
card.notSee: The planet and brown-dwarf companions are invisible to amateur instruments.
card.deeper: Matthews et al. (2024) imaged ε Indi Ab with JWST/MIRI at 10.65 and 15.5 µm: a planet of a few Jupiter masses at about 275 K, on a wider orbit than radial-velocity solutions predicted. The star lies at 3.6384 ± 0.0013 pc; published ages span about 3.5–5.7 Gyr. Solar-like oscillations give 0.782 ± 0.023 M☉ (Lundkvist et al. 2024). A pair of brown dwarfs, ε Ind Ba/Bb, orbits far out.

distanceLy.note: 64 pc adopted; Hipparcos 15.61 ± 0.99 mas, Gaia EDR3 17.79 ± 0.82 mas

superlatives.claim: one of the nearest stars in the final giant stage (the asymptotic giant branch)

historyHook.text: ESO’s VLT revealed a dusty disk and a close companion around it: the earliest stage of a butterfly-shaped planetary nebula.

images.caption: VLT/SPHERE image of the dust disk around L² Puppis, seen almost edge-on; the star itself is hidden behind the dark lane.

card.question: What will the Sun look like near the very end of its giant life?
card.glance: A reddish variable star in Puppis that can be easy or faint depending on the year.
card.whyHere: L² Puppis is a star of about the Sun’s mass near the very end of its giant life, a preview of the Sun’s distant future.
card.see: Find L² Puppis about 7.5° south of Pi Puppis, where it forms a wide pair with its blue-white neighbor L¹ Puppis. In binoculars L² is clearly redder, so check its brightness against L¹ on different nights.
card.understand: L² Puppis is shedding its outer layers in a slow, dusty wind, and it pulses every 140 days or so while its dust can dim it for years. ALMA, an array of radio dishes, watched the gas swirling close to the star and, from how fast it circles, weighed the star at about two-thirds of the Sun’s mass. The Sun will pass through this stage before leaving a small, hot core behind.
card.wonder: ESO’s VLT has seen a dusty disk and a close companion around it, the first stirrings of a butterfly-shaped planetary nebula.
card.connect: When the dust clears, the exposed core will light up the shed gas as a glowing shell, a planetary nebula.
card.answer: Much like L² Puppis, a dying giant of about the Sun’s mass, pulsing and wrapping itself in dust as it lets its outer layers go, which astronomers call a flash-forward of our own Sun by 5 to 6 billion years.
card.photoCaption: The VLT photo shows a dusty disk seen edge-on; binoculars show only a reddish point.
card.notSee: The disk and companion are invisible in binoculars.
card.deeper: ALMA observations resolved the rotating gas close to the star and gave 0.659 ± 0.011 ± 0.041 M☉ for L² Pup A, plus a candidate companion about 2 au away (Kervella et al. 2016). NACO aperture masking showed a dusty torus with an inner radius of about 4.2 au (Lykou et al. 2015). VSX lists a semiregular period of 140.6 d and a range of 2.6–8.0 mag; the faint end reflects dust episodes since the 1990s, so present brightness cannot be predicted offline.

eventDependent.note: Dust can dim it for years; check AAVSO for its current brightness rather than assuming it is easy.

card.question: Why is the red star of the Crane cooler than the white one beside it?
card.glance: The orange-red star of Grus, the Crane, six degrees from blue-white Alnair, a ready-made color contrast.
card.whyHere: Tiaki is one half of the finest naked-eye color pair in the far-southern sky, a cool red giant beside a hot blue-white star.
card.see: Put Tiaki and Alnair in turn at the center of your binoculars: Tiaki is a deep orange-red, Alnair a clean blue-white. Defocus slightly and the colors strengthen, and over weeks you can watch Tiaki’s brightness wander a little.
card.understand: Tiaki is a red giant near the end of its life, swollen to about 150 times the Sun’s width. Its surface is only about 3,500 K, so it glows orange-red. Blacksmiths know the rule: iron glows red first and white only when far hotter, and stars follow the same physics.
card.wonder: Its swollen outer layers heave on a rough rhythm of about 37 days, nudging its brightness up and down.
card.connect: Its puffed-up outer layers are already drifting away, and L² Puppis shows a star further down the same road.
card.answer: In stars, color is a thermometer that runs opposite to the bathroom tap, so red Tiaki is the cool one, far cooler than blue-white Alnair beside it.
card.photoCaption: Photos exaggerate star sizes; the colors are real, and binoculars show them well on bright stars.
card.deeper: An SED fit with the Hipparcos distance (54 pc) gives about 3,500 K, 3,200 L☉ and 154 R☉ (McDonald et al. 2017). VSX classes it as a semiregular variable (SRb) with a 37-day period and a range of 1.9–2.3 mag. Its spectral type (M4.5 III) and luminosity are typical of a star climbing the asymptotic giant branch. Its IAU name, Tiaki, comes from Polynesian tradition.

distanceLy.note: parallax 7.16 ± 0.21 mas; IC 2602 cluster distance 491 ly (Hunt & Reffert 2024)

card.question: Which looks brighter, a nearby cluster star or a distant monster?
card.glance: The brightest star of the Southern Pleiades in Carina, a scatter of blue-white stars that fills a binocular view.
card.whyHere: Theta Carinae is the leading light of a nearby star family, and its neighbor Eta Carinae turns brightness upside down.
card.see: Theta Carinae is the brightest of a loose group of blue-white stars visible even to the naked eye. In binoculars the group spreads over about a degree, with dozens of fainter members, and about 5° north lie the Carina Nebula and Eta Carinae.
card.understand: The Southern Pleiades is an open cluster, a family of stars born together, tens of millions of years old and about 490 light-years away. Theta Carinae is its brightest and hottest member. Eta Carinae looks fainter from here, yet it is more than 15 times farther away, so it must be vastly more powerful.
card.wonder: Seen from a planet near Eta Carinae, this whole cluster would be too faint to notice.
card.connect: Swing north to Eta Carinae and compare: the fainter-looking star is the true giant.
card.answer: The nearby star wins to the eye: Theta Carinae, about 456 light-years away, outshines Eta Carinae, although Eta Carinae is the true giant, because apparent brightness always mixes power with distance.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the cluster as a spray of blue-white stars; binoculars give a very similar view.
card.deeper: θ Car (B0 V, spectroscopic binary) is the brightest star in the field of IC 2602, whose Gaia DR3 members give a distance of about 150 pc (Hunt & Reffert 2024) and whose lithium-depletion age is about 46 Myr (Dobbie et al. 2010). Its Hipparcos parallax (7.16 ± 0.21 mas, ~455 ly) is slightly nearer than the cluster mean; Gaia does not measure stars this bright well. An early-B star in a cluster this old would be unexpected for a normal single star, so its history may involve a companion.

ageMyr.note: YREC 6.46 ± 0.13 Gyr; range across analyses 6.1–7.5 Gyr

card.question: What will the Sun be like a few billion years from now?
card.glance: A modest yellowish star in Hydrus near the south celestial pole, close to the Small Magellanic Cloud.
card.whyHere: Beta Hydri is an older, slightly heavier Sun-like star that has begun to swell, a look at the Sun’s next chapter.
card.see: Beta Hydri sits near the south celestial pole, roughly between the Small Magellanic Cloud and the pole. Binoculars show a soft yellow star, the tint the Sun would show at night, and about 5° away lies the Small Cloud’s misty glow.
card.understand: Beta Hydri rings gently like a bell, its surface rising and falling in tiny oscillations that the TESS satellite detected in its light. The pitch of those tones depends on the star’s size and density, so they weigh and date it: about 1.1 Suns of mass and about 6.5 billion years old. It has finished burning hydrogen in its core and is slowly swelling, already almost twice the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: It also has a 12-year cycle of magnetic activity, much like the Sun’s own.
card.connect: Further down the Sun’s road lie bigger, shedding giants such as L² Puppis.
card.answer: Much like Beta Hydri, an older Sun already over three times as bright as ours, a stage our own star will reach in a few billion years.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a plain yellowish star; its swelling is measured through its oscillations and interferometry.
card.deeper: TESS detected solar-like oscillations; five independent model fits agree on 1.06–1.13 M☉, 1.80–1.84 R☉ and 6.1–7.5 Gyr (Metcalfe et al. 2024; earlier modeling by Brandão et al. 2011). The star has left the main sequence and burns hydrogen in a shell around its helium core. Metcalfe et al. also report a 12-year activity cycle, unusual for a star this evolved.

multiplicity.systemNote: The bright eclipsing pair Aa–Ab has a 1″ companion B and a distant common-motion pair C–D (WDS).

superlatives.claim: one of the brightest eclipsing binaries, recognized only in 2000

historyHook.text: Its eclipses were caught by an amateur’s eye in 1997 and in the star-tracker data of NASA’s Galileo probe, which used it to steer.

card.question: How could a bright star hide its eclipses for all of history?
card.glance: One corner of the False Cross, a bright white star that dims for some hours every few weeks.
card.whyHere: Delta Velorum was quietly eclipsing for all of history, unnoticed until the year 2000.
card.see: Find the False Cross in Vela and Carina, a larger, fainter look-alike of the Southern Cross, and Delta Velorum is one of its four corners. On most nights it is clearly brighter than Kappa Velorum and Aspidiske, and during an eclipse it drops to about their level.
card.understand: Delta Velorum is two white stars orbiting each other every 45 days, and our view runs almost along their orbit, so once per orbit one passes in front of the other: an eclipsing binary. Each dip lasts only hours and costs less than half a magnitude, so in most years you would have to be watching at just the right time. An amateur caught one by eye in 1997, and the star-tracker of NASA’s Galileo probe, which used the star to steer, had recorded others.
card.wonder: Earth’s slowly wobbling axis is carrying the south celestial pole toward it, and around the year 9000 Delta Velorum will serve as a southern pole star.
card.connect: The False Cross fools navigators, and its stars are not even close together: Avior is roughly seven times farther away.
card.answer: Its eclipses are rare and brief, one short dip per orbit, and they slipped past generations of observers until 2000, when the two records were put together. Even the brightest stars can keep a secret.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a bright white point; eclipses are seen by comparing its brightness with nearby stars.
card.deeper: Otero, Fieseler & Lloyd (2000) reported a ~0.3 mag fading seen visually in 1997 and in Galileo star-scanner engineering data (1989, 2000); Hipparcos had missed the eclipses. Their ephemeris gives P = 45.150 ± 0.001 d with unequal primary and secondary minima (eccentric orbit). The bright pair has a 1″ companion (F8 V), and Hipparcos places the system at 40.5 mas (81 ly).

eventDependent.note: Eclipses last about a day every 45 days; the app should show predicted eclipse dates rather than a fixed brightness.

radiusRsun.note: JSDC photometric diameter 11.91 ± 1.37 mas × Hipparcos distance

card.question: How can a cool star also be enormously bright?
card.glance: A bright orange star in Vela, glowing like an ember among blue-white neighbors.
card.whyHere: Suhail is a supergiant, cool, orange and enormous, the biggest star in this part of Vela.
card.see: Suhail is the bright orange star about 11° east-north-east of Gamma Velorum. Defocus a little to make its color glow, then swing to blue-white Gamma Velorum to read the temperature difference.
card.understand: Suhail is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with a surface near 3,900 K. A cooler surface gives off less light per square meter, so a cool star can only be this bright by having an enormous number of square meters. Its total light, gathered across all colors and combined with its distance, reveals the size: about 200 times the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: Put it where the Sun is and its surface would reach almost to Earth’s orbit.
card.connect: Gamma Velorum and Naos, not far away, show hotter chapters in the lives of heavy stars.
card.answer: Each patch of Suhail is dimmer than the Sun’s surface, but there is so much of it that the star gives out nearly 9,000 times the Sun’s light.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point; the color in binoculars is real.
card.deeper: Hipparcos gives 5.99 ± 0.11 mas (≈545 ly). An SED fit (McDonald et al. 2017) gives ~3,900 K and ~8,700 L☉; the JSDC photometric diameter (11.9 ± 1.4 mas) implies about 210 R☉ (≈1 au, so ‘almost to Earth’s orbit’ given the ±12% uncertainty). GCVS classes it as a slow irregular variable (Lc), 2.14–2.30 mag.

card.question: What is the second star hiding inside Alpha Centauri?
card.glance: Hidden inside the same point of light as Alpha Centauri A, too close for binoculars to separate.
card.whyHere: Alpha Centauri B is the orange half of our nearest naked-eye star system, a slightly smaller, cooler cousin of the Sun.
card.see: Aim at Alpha Centauri: B is inside that single bright point, adding a touch of orange. Only a telescope at high power shows two stars.
card.understand: The orbit of A and B weighs them, because the size and period of an orbit fix the total mass and each star’s swing sets its share. B has about 97 percent of the Sun’s mass. Its surface is near 5,200 K, cooler than the Sun’s, so it shines orange.
card.wonder: From a planet around B, Alpha Centauri A would blaze far brighter than our full Moon.
card.connect: Same birth, same age, different mass: mass sets a star’s color and brightness.
card.answer: Alpha Centauri B, an orange star almost as massive as the Sun, too close to its partner for binoculars to split, and that small shortfall in mass is enough to change its color.
card.photoCaption: Photos merge A and B into one glare; a telescope shows the orange B beside yellow-white A.

distanceLy.note: parallax 10.13 ± 0.5 mas; combined α Cru system (HIP 60718)

card.question: How many stars make up Acrux?
card.glance: The fainter half of Acrux, which binoculars merge with its partner into one star.
card.whyHere: Alpha² Crucis is the second bright star inside Acrux, a hot blue-white star of the same system.
card.see: Center Acrux at the foot of the Southern Cross. Its two bright stars sit a hair’s breadth apart, so binoculars show one point while a small telescope shows two.
card.understand: Like its partner, Alpha² Crucis is a hot, heavy young star whose blue-white color marks a surface far hotter than the Sun’s. The other bright star has a secret of its own. Its spectral lines shift back and forth on a regular rhythm, the signature of an unseen companion.
card.wonder: Each of the two would rank among the brighter stars of the sky on its own.
card.connect: Acrux’s wider family spreads across the whole Southern Cross.
card.answer: There are at least three, two bright blue-white stars a hair’s breadth apart, the brighter of them itself a close pair.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split Acrux into two blue-white stars; binoculars cannot.

card.question: What do stars a little heavier than the Sun become?
card.glance: The brightest star of Phoenix, a pale orange point in a sparse part of the sky.
card.whyHere: Ankaa is an orange giant, a common late stage for stars a little heavier than the Sun.
card.see: Ankaa stands alone between Achernar and Fomalhaut. In binoculars notice its pale orange color compared with blue-white Achernar.
card.understand: Ankaa has left its long, steady adult life behind. With its core hydrogen used up, it swelled to about 15 times the Sun’s width, and its larger surface cooled to about 4,500 K. Its total light and its distance together reveal that size, since a cool star can only shine this brightly by being large.
card.wonder: Its light left about 85 years ago, around when the first jet aircraft flew.
card.connect: Achernar, hot and young, shows a very different stage of a star’s life.
card.answer: They become orange giants like Ankaa, swollen and cooled after their steady adult years, and because this calm stage lasts so long, many bright stars are giants like this.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a pale orange point; the color in binoculars is subtle but real.

card.question: Why does Achernar look brighter than nearer Alpha Hydri?
card.glance: A creamy white star 5° from Achernar.
card.whyHere: Alpha Hydri is a nearby white star and a handy comparison for blue-white Achernar.
card.see: Put Achernar and Alpha Hydri in the same sweep, about 5° apart. Achernar looks icy blue-white, Alpha Hydri slightly warmer and creamier.
card.understand: Alpha Hydri is a little hotter and heavier than the Sun, at about 7,100 K, and only about 63 light-years away. Achernar is far hotter and about six times the Sun’s mass. Heavy stars are disproportionately bright, so a star like Achernar outshines a modest one many times over.
card.wonder: The light you see left it in the mid-1960s, about when the first spacecraft sent back close-up pictures of Mars.
card.connect: Beta Hydri, nearer the pole, is a star like an older Sun.
card.answer: Achernar is simply far more powerful, so although it lies more than twice as far away, its hot, heavy bulk easily outshines creamy Alpha Hydri.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point; its color differs only slightly from Achernar’s.

card.question: Which star points the way to a runaway from Orion?
card.glance: The brightest star of Columba, the Dove, a blue-white point south of Lepus.
card.whyHere: Phact is a hot, fast-spinning star and the signpost to the runaway Mu Columbae.
card.see: Phact is easy to the naked eye. Put it near the edge of your binocular view, and Mu Columbae is the fainter bluish star about 2° to the north-east.
card.understand: Phact is a Be star, a hot blue star that spins fast enough to shed a thin disk of gas from its equator. That disk glows, adding bright lines to its spectrum, which is how such stars are recognized. Its distance, from Gaia’s parallax, is about 286 light-years.
card.wonder: Mu Columbae looks much fainter, yet it lies over six times farther away and far outshines Phact.
card.connect: Mu Columbae, a star thrown out of Orion, is a short hop away.
card.answer: Phact, the brightest star of Columba: about 2° north-east of it lies Mu Columbae, flung out of the Orion Nebula’s cluster. Phact is the easy step toward a star with a remarkable past.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point; its gas disk is detected only in spectra.

card.question: What kind of star is Tau Puppis?
card.glance: A yellow-orange star in southern Puppis, between Canopus and the Milky Way.
card.whyHere: Tau Puppis is an orange giant with a close companion, a typical aging star near brilliant Canopus.
card.see: In binoculars Tau Puppis is a soft yellow-orange point. Compare it with brilliant white Canopus about 5° to the west-south-west.
card.understand: Tau Puppis is a giant about 25 times the Sun’s width, with a cooler surface near 4,600 K. Its companion is too close to see, revealed only by the shifting lines in its spectrum. Stars like it are in a long, settled phase after their core hydrogen ran out.
card.wonder: Canopus beside it is a far heavier giant, though both have left their steady adult lives behind.
card.connect: Canopus, nearby, is a far more powerful giant.
card.answer: An aging orange giant about 25 times the Sun’s width, quietly orbited by a companion no telescope can split. It is the kind of star the sky is full of once you start looking.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a yellow-orange point.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun shine 11,000 times brighter?
card.glance: A deep yellow-orange star in Puppis with a faint companion close by.
card.whyHere: Pi Puppis is the cool end of the Puppis thermometer, an orange supergiant 10° from blue-white Naos.
card.see: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange, and at 10× a much fainter star separates just to its south-west, easier still on a tripod, though at 7× it usually drowns in the glare. Then swing about 10° east to Naos for the color contrast.
card.understand: Pi Puppis is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with a surface near 3,900 K. Each square meter of a surface that cool gives out only a fraction of the Sun’s light. Its total light, measured across all colors and scaled by distance, still comes to about 11,000 Suns, leaving one way to balance the books.
card.wonder: It is the brightest member of a loose young cluster scattered around it, which binoculars show as a sprinkle of fainter stars.
card.connect: Ten degrees east, Naos burns ten times hotter.
card.answer: It must be vast, and it is, about 230 times the Sun’s width, so its sheer extent makes up for its coolness.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point with faint neighbors; the color is real.

card.question: Can a star’s brightness change within a few hours?
card.glance: A yellow-white star in northern Puppis that pulses every few hours.
card.whyHere: Tureis is a star you could, in principle, watch breathe in a single night.
card.see: In binoculars Tureis is a plain yellow-white point. Its brightness rises and falls by about a fifth every three and a half hours, too little to judge easily by eye.
card.understand: Tureis is a pulsating star whose outer layers swell and shrink in a steady rhythm. As the star expands and contracts, its surface heats and cools slightly, changing its brightness. Instruments time the beat precisely, and the rhythm is as regular as a clock.
card.wonder: It belongs to the same pulsing family as δ Scuti, stars whose outer layers trap and release heat like a valve.
card.connect: Other stars change far more, through eclipses, dust or wild outbursts.
card.answer: It can, as Tureis swells and shrinks about seven times a day, changing its brightness by about a fifth.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a yellow-white point; its pulsing shows up only in measurements.

card.question: Why is one corner of the False Cross orange?
card.glance: The orange corner of the False Cross, in Carina.
card.whyHere: Avior is a blend of two stars, an orange giant and a hot blue star, that looks like one orange point.
card.see: Avior is the brightest star of the False Cross and the only one with a clear orange tint. Compare it with white Delta Velorum and Aspidiske.
card.understand: Spread Avior’s light into a spectrum and two sets of fingerprints appear, those of a cool orange giant and those of a hotter blue star. The giant is the more luminous in visible light, so it sets the color. The two are too close to split with any binoculars.
card.wonder: It is roughly seven times farther away than Delta Velorum, its partner in the False Cross.
card.connect: The False Cross is a pattern of stars at very different distances.
card.answer: Avior’s light blends two stars, and the cool orange giant outshines its hot blue companion, so the mixture looks orange, two colors blended into one point.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single orange point.

card.question: How far apart are a bright star and the star swarm beside it?
card.glance: A bright white star deep in the southern sky, in Carina, south-west of the Southern Pleiades.
card.whyHere: Miaplacidus is a bright white star near the end of its adult life, and a stepping stone to a globular cluster nearby.
card.see: Miaplacidus shines bright white about 5° south of the globular cluster NGC 2808. In binoculars compare the sharp star with the cluster’s soft glow.
card.understand: Miaplacidus is a white star heavier than the Sun, close to the end of its long hydrogen-burning life. Its parallax, the shift as Earth circles the Sun, puts it about 113 light-years away. The cluster beside it is far too remote for that shift to show.
card.wonder: Its light set out before anyone knew that other galaxies existed.
card.connect: From a near star to a distant swarm of ancient ones is a single hop.
card.answer: Enormously far: the globular cluster NGC 2808 sent its light some 33,000 years ago, so it and Miaplacidus share a field of view and almost nothing else.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a bright white point.

card.question: Are the corners of the False Cross neighbors in space?
card.glance: A white corner of the False Cross, in Carina.
card.whyHere: Aspidiske is one of the four corners of the False Cross, and the way to test whether those corners are neighbors.
card.see: Aspidiske marks one corner of the False Cross. It looks about as bright as Delta Velorum on most nights.
card.understand: Aspidiske is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, about 47 times the Sun’s width and about 5,000 times its light. Its parallax puts it about 770 light-years away. To look as bright as nearby Delta Velorum from that far, it must be vastly more luminous.
card.wonder: Its light set out around the year 1260, when Marco Polo was still a boy.
card.connect: Kappa Velorum, at the next corner, makes a handy gauge for catching Delta Velorum in eclipse.
card.answer: Aspidiske looks about as bright as Delta Velorum but is a supergiant almost ten times farther away, so the False Cross is drawn with stars at very different depths.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point.

card.question: How can you tell when Delta Velorum is in eclipse?
card.glance: A blue-white corner of the False Cross, in Vela.
card.whyHere: Kappa Velorum is a hot blue-white star and a handy comparison star for Delta Velorum’s eclipses.
card.see: Kappa Velorum is the dimmest corner of the False Cross. Use it as a yardstick for Delta Velorum.
card.understand: Kappa Velorum is a hot young star, much heavier and more luminous than the Sun, about 570 light-years away. Eyes judge brightness poorly on their own but compare two stars well, so a steady neighbor makes a good gauge. Kappa sits close to Delta’s eclipse level.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time Gutenberg was printing his first books.
card.connect: Check Delta Velorum against it tonight.
card.answer: Compare the two, because when Delta Velorum sinks to Kappa’s brightness an eclipse is under way, while on most nights Delta is clearly the brighter.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Can a giant and a Sun-like star share one orbit?
card.glance: A yellow star in Vela, north of the Carina Nebula region.
card.whyHere: Mu Velorum is a yellow giant with a Sun-like companion, two stages of life side by side.
card.see: Mu Velorum is a plain yellow point in binoculars. Its Sun-like companion lies too close to split without a telescope.
card.understand: The two stars were probably born together, but the giant started out heavier. Heavier stars use up their core hydrogen sooner, so it has already swollen while its partner is still a Sun-like dwarf. One system now holds two chapters of the same story.
card.wonder: Its light left about 112 years ago, around when the First World War began.
card.connect: Giants are a phase every Sun-like star passes through.
card.answer: They can, and Mu Velorum is a yellow giant that has left its steady adult life, circled by a companion still in the Sun’s stage, two siblings moving at different paces.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single yellow point.

card.question: Why does Delta Centauri’s brightness drift over months?
card.glance: A blue-white star north-west of the Southern Cross, with two fainter stars nearby in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Delta Centauri is a fast-spinning Be star that sheds disks of gas, set in a pretty binocular triangle.
card.see: In binoculars Delta Centauri forms a wide group with two fainter stars close beside it. Its brightness drifts slightly over months.
card.understand: Delta Centauri is a Be star, a hot blue star spinning so fast that gas leaks from its equator into a thin disk. The disk glows and adds its own light, so as it builds and dissipates, the total shifts. Its spectrum shows bright lines from the disk, the signature of its class.
card.wonder: It probably belongs to the same young star family as Delta Crucis, about 16 million years old.
card.connect: Achernar, far across the sky, is a closer member of the same spinning class.
card.answer: Its disk comes and goes: as the gas spun off its equator gathers and thins, the star’s combined light wanders. You are watching weather on a scale of solar systems.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white star with two fainter neighbors, relatives from the same young family rather than partners in an orbit.

card.question: Where are the Southern Cross’s brothers and sisters?
card.glance: The faintest of the Southern Cross’s four main stars, on its western arm.
card.whyHere: Delta Crucis is a confirmed member of the scattered young family that the Southern Cross’s blue stars belong to.
card.see: Delta Crucis is the dimmest star of the Cross. Compare its blue-white with orange Gacrux at the top.
card.understand: Delta Crucis was born with thousands of other stars about 16 million years ago in an association, a loose family that has since spread across Crux and Centaurus. The members are recognized by their shared motion, like a flock of birds that has scattered but still flies the same way. Delta Crucis fits that motion well.
card.wonder: It pulses gently every few hours, a trait it shares with several of its hot siblings.
card.connect: Gacrux, at the top of the Cross, is not part of this family.
card.answer: They are scattered across Crux, Centaurus and beyond, still drifting the same way through space though they no longer look like a cluster, so the family is all around the Cross.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Does the Southern Cross family reach beyond the Cross?
card.glance: The brightest star of Musca, the Fly, just south of the Southern Cross.
card.whyHere: Alpha Muscae is another sibling of the Southern Cross family, a short hop south of Acrux.
card.see: Alpha Muscae is a blue-white star about 6° south of Acrux. Its color matches Acrux and Mimosa, a hint that they are related.
card.understand: It belongs to the same scattered family of young stars as Delta Crucis, born about 16 million years ago. Its motion through space matches theirs, which is how membership is decided. Like several of its siblings, it is hot and heavy.
card.wonder: It flickers in brightness every two hours or so, by an amount far too small to see.
card.connect: Back north, the Coalsack’s dark cloud lies between the Fly and the Cross.
card.answer: It does, for Alpha Muscae shares the Cross stars’ blue-white color and their motion, a sibling just outside the famous pattern, since constellation lines do not bound families.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Can one star turn out to be a pair of twins?
card.glance: A white star in Centaurus, north of the Southern Cross.
card.whyHere: Gamma Centauri is a pair of near-identical white stars, too close to split in binoculars.
card.see: Gamma Centauri is a steady white point in binoculars. Its two equal stars sit far too close together for binoculars, or even most telescopes.
card.understand: Two stars of nearly the same mass and temperature orbit each other here. Their combined spectrum shows two matching sets of lines, and only careful measurement separates them. Binaries like this are common; the Sun’s single life is the less usual arrangement.
card.wonder: Its light takes about 130 years to reach you, so it set out around when X-rays were discovered.
card.connect: Most stars have partners, and many are far too close to see.
card.answer: Gamma Centauri is exactly that, two near-identical white stars orbiting far too close together for binoculars to split.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single white point.

card.question: How do you climb a distance ladder to another galaxy?
card.glance: A white star in northern Centaurus, about 6° from the galaxy Centaurus A.
card.whyHere: Iota Centauri is a nearby white star that makes a perfect first rung on a distance ladder to a galaxy.
card.see: Iota Centauri is a plain white point. About 6° south lies Centaurus A, a faint galaxy smudge, and Omega Centauri’s glow is about 11° away.
card.understand: Each rung of a distance ladder uses a method that works only within a certain range. Parallax handles nearby stars like this one, only about 58 light-years away. Farther rungs rely on stars of known brightness, calibrated with parallax, which in turn reach clusters and galaxies.
card.wonder: From Centaurus A, our entire galaxy would look like a faint smudge, much as that galaxy looks to you.
card.connect: Omega Centauri, a ball of millions of stars, is the next rung, then a whole galaxy.
card.answer: One rung at a time, from Iota Centauri through Omega Centauri to Centaurus A, 6° south and about 200,000 times farther, with every rung resting on the one below.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point.

card.question: How much farther is Omega Centauri than the bright star beside it?
card.glance: A bright blue-white star in Centaurus, between Hadar and a great star cluster.
card.whyHere: Epsilon Centauri is a hot young star of the Centaurus family, and a stepping stone toward Omega Centauri.
card.see: Epsilon Centauri is the bright blue-white star between Hadar and the fuzzy ball of Omega Centauri. The cluster lies about 6° away.
card.understand: Epsilon Centauri is a heavy young star that pulses slightly every few hours. Its parallax puts it about 427 light-years away. Omega Centauri is too far for parallax to help much, so its distance comes from its stars’ brightness and motions.
card.wonder: Its whole life will be over long before the oldest stars in Omega Centauri have aged noticeably.
card.connect: The cluster’s soft glow is a short hop away.
card.answer: Omega Centauri is about 40 times farther, a swarm of ancient stars far beyond this young one, so two neighbors on the sky are separated by most of the galaxy’s history.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: What separates a young star from the ancient swarm beside it?
card.glance: A blue-white star about 5° from Omega Centauri.
card.whyHere: Zeta Centauri is a young star beside an ancient star swarm, and a handy signpost to Omega Centauri.
card.see: Zeta Centauri sits about 5° east of Omega Centauri. Put both in turn in your view: a sharp young star, then a soft ball of ancient ones.
card.understand: Zeta Centauri is a hot young binary whose two stars circle every eight days. Its age shows in its color and power, since only young stars can be this hot and heavy. Omega Centauri’s stars are the opposite, small and old, the heavy ones long gone.
card.wonder: Its light left about 380 years ago, while Omega Centauri’s set out before anyone on Earth had planted a crop.
card.connect: The swarm itself is next door.
card.answer: Both age and distance separate them, for Omega Centauri is a ball of ancient stars over 45 times farther away than this hot young binary.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: What will Sun-like stars look like as giants?
card.glance: A pale orange star in northern Centaurus.
card.whyHere: Menkent is a fairly close orange giant, a preview of a later stage in the life of Sun-like stars.
card.see: Menkent is a pale orange point in binoculars. Compare it with the blue-white stars of southern Centaurus.
card.understand: Menkent has run through its core hydrogen and swollen to about 11 times the Sun’s width. Its surface cooled as it grew, shifting its color toward orange. Iota Centauri lies at almost the same distance, so the two make a fair comparison of a giant and a star still in its prime.
card.wonder: Its light left about 59 years ago, around when surgeons in Cape Town performed the first heart transplant.
card.connect: Further south, far hotter and younger stars wait.
card.answer: Much like Menkent, a pale orange giant, a stage the Sun itself will reach in billions of years.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a pale orange point.

card.question: Why does Eta Centauri’s brightness wander?
card.glance: A blue-white star in eastern Centaurus.
card.whyHere: Eta Centauri is a spinning Be star whose brightness wanders as it sheds gas.
card.see: Eta Centauri is a blue-white point in binoculars. Its brightness varies a little over weeks to months.
card.understand: Like Achernar and Delta Centauri, it is a Be star, a hot blue star spinning fast enough to fling gas into a disk around its equator. The disk adds its own glow, so the star’s total light depends on how much gas is there. Its spectrum shows bright lines from that disk.
card.wonder: Its light left about 300 years ago, while Edmond Halley was still waiting for his comet to come back.
card.connect: Spinning stars come in many sizes, and Achernar is among the most flattened we know.
card.answer: Its gas disk keeps changing, and the star’s light changes with it over weeks to months. The star is steady; its skirt is not.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Are the three stars of the Southern Triangle alike?
card.glance: A white corner of the Southern Triangle, Triangulum Australe.
card.whyHere: Gamma Trianguli Australis is the white corner of a triangle whose three stars all differ in color and distance.
card.see: Compare the three corners of the Southern Triangle: orange Atria, creamy Beta and white Gamma. Gamma is the one at the triangle’s western tip.
card.understand: Gamma Trianguli Australis is a hot white star, hotter than either of its partners. Its parallax puts it about 190 light-years away. The three corners have different temperatures and lie at different depths.
card.wonder: If you could fly around the triangle, its shape would collapse and rearrange itself.
card.connect: Orange Atria makes the color contrast.
card.answer: The corners differ in color and lie at about 40, 190 and 390 light-years, with white Gamma in the middle, so a neat triangle in the sky is a scattered trio in space.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point.

card.question: Why does nearby Beta look about as bright as distant Atria?
card.glance: A creamy white corner of the Southern Triangle.
card.whyHere: Beta Trianguli Australis looks nearly as bright as Atria, though it is about ten times closer.
card.see: Swing between Beta and Atria. Atria looks a little brighter and orange, Beta creamy white.
card.understand: Beta Trianguli Australis is a modest star only a little hotter than the Sun, about 40 light-years away. Atria lies about ten times farther. Light fades with the square of distance, so from ten times as far, Atria must be about a hundred times more powerful just to keep up.
card.wonder: Moved this close, Atria would outshine every star in the sky.
card.connect: Atria, the triangle’s orange corner, is a giant many times wider than the Sun.
card.answer: Atria is simply far more powerful: from ten times farther away it still looks a little brighter, so it must shine hundreds of times brighter than Beta.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a creamy white point.

radiusRsun.note: VLTI/AMBER diameter 9.24 mas (Cruzalèbes et al. 2013) × Hipparcos distance

card.question: What makes Atria the brightest corner of its triangle?
card.glance: The bright orange corner of the Southern Triangle.
card.whyHere: Atria is an orange giant about 120 times the Sun’s width, and the brightest corner of its triangle.
card.see: Atria is a vivid orange point. Defocus slightly to enhance the color, then compare it with the white corners of the triangle.
card.understand: Interferometers at the VLT measured Atria’s tiny disk, and with its distance that gives about 120 times the Sun’s width. Its surface is cool, near 4,300 K. A surface that big glows with nearly 4,000 times the Sun’s light even at that cool temperature.
card.wonder: Its light left about 390 years ago, around when Galileo was put on trial for saying that the Earth moves.
card.connect: Beta, the triangle’s creamy corner, looks almost as bright from ten times closer.
card.answer: Its sheer size does it, for Atria’s vast orange surface outshines its smaller, hotter neighbors, making the farthest corner the brightest.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point; the color is real.

card.question: What lights the far-southern sky in Pavo?
card.glance: A lone blue-white star in the far-southern constellation of the Peacock.
card.whyHere: The Peacock is a hot blue-white star and a close binary, a lighthouse of the far-southern sky.
card.see: The Peacock is the bright blue-white star of Pavo. Binoculars show a sharp point with a few faint field stars around it.
card.understand: It is a hot young star much heavier than the Sun. Its companion is too close to see, revealed only in its spectrum, the star’s light spread into colors, where the lines shift back and forth with each orbit. Few bright stars lie near it, so it stands out.
card.wonder: Its light left about 180 years ago, around when the first photograph of a star was taken.
card.connect: Epsilon Indi looks much fainter, yet it is fifteen times closer.
card.answer: The Peacock does, a hot young blue-white star with a hidden companion, shining alone in a dark region that makes it a natural landmark.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Why is Alnair blue-white beside orange-red Tiaki?
card.glance: The brightest star of Grus, the Crane, blue-white and six degrees from orange-red Tiaki.
card.whyHere: Alnair is the hot half of a naked-eye color pair, best seen beside Tiaki.
card.see: Center Alnair, then Tiaki: one is blue-white, the other orange-red. Defocusing both slightly makes the colors richer.
card.understand: Alnair is a hot young star with a surface several times hotter than the Sun’s, so it shines blue-white. Hotter surfaces send out more of their light at shorter, bluer wavelengths. Tiaki’s cool surface does the opposite.
card.wonder: Tiaki is cooler, yet gives out far more light because it is so large.
card.connect: Swing back to Tiaki and read the thermometer.
card.answer: Its surface is several times hotter than the Sun’s, while Tiaki’s is cooler. Tiaki still gives out more light because it is a giant, a reminder that color reads temperature, not power.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: What is the orange star on the way to the Small Magellanic Cloud?
card.glance: An orange star in Tucana, between Grus and the Small Magellanic Cloud.
card.whyHere: Alpha Tucanae is an orange giant with a close companion, on the way to the Small Magellanic Cloud.
card.see: Alpha Tucanae is a soft orange point in binoculars. It stands alone in a quiet field.
card.understand: Alpha Tucanae is a giant whose surface has cooled to about 4,200 K. A companion circles it, too close to see. Its total light and distance together put its width at about 38 times the Sun’s.
card.wonder: Its light left about 180 years ago, around when Neptune was discovered.
card.connect: Follow Tucana south to the Small Magellanic Cloud and 47 Tucanae.
card.answer: Alpha Tucanae, an orange giant with a cool surface and a hidden companion. It is a stepping stone from our neighborhood to another galaxy.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point.

contexts.name: Lower Centaurus–Crux (Sco-Cen)

ageMyr.note: mean age of LCC (and UCL) ≈ 16 Myr

contexts.text: The southernmost subgroup of the Sco-Cen family: hot young stars scattered across Crux, Musca and Centaurus, born about 16 million years ago. δ Cru and α Mus are secure members; Mimosa and δ Cen probable; Acrux, Hadar and ε Cen debated.
